en: Read One Route Through Gansu Provincial Museum
zh: 在甘肃省博物馆读一条路
ja: 甘粛省博物館で一本の道を読む

p.src: Enter the forecourt from the Xijin West Road side and identify the long pale-stone frontage, the raised central entrance, and the vertical window bays. The four guides near the entrance make the building's breadth easier to judge. Set aside a fresh half-day for Gansu Provincial Museum rather than squeezing it into time left after a river walk. Inside, check which galleries and key objects are available before committing to the route. The collections come from across Gansu. Their presence in Lanzhou does not make them Lanzhou finds. Follow one line today: begin with the form, pattern, and findspot of prehistoric painted pottery; move to Buddhist images and reliquary containers; then compare a horse's image of speed with the messengers and travel documents that made actual passage possible. The entrance is where the province first comes into view.

caption.zh: 灰白石材的长立面围住中央入口。先认建筑，再在门厅确认当天展厅与重点文物。
caption.ja: 淡い石張りの長い正面に中央入口が開く。建物を確認し、館内で当日の展示室と主要資料を確かめる。
caption.en: A long pale-stone frontage frames the central entrance. Recognize the building, then confirm today's galleries and key objects inside.

p.src: As checked on 22 August 2026, the official guide lists Tuesday-Sunday opening from 09:00 to 17:00, appointment cutoff at 16:00, and last entry at 16:30. Monday is closed except for statutory holidays or a special notice. Individual admission is free and may be booked up to three days ahead through the museum's two named WeChat accounts. The same official record gives two different daily release times, so this guide does not guess which one applies; check the current appointment screen before leaving. Bring the original identity document used for the booking. Passports are on the accepted list. Store large bags first. Ask about a staff-led tour at the first-floor west service desk; the museum says this service is not sold online. Use Metro Line 1 for orientation and follow current exit signs. Do not use flash, a selfie stick, or a tripod in the galleries.

p.src: This is not a room-level floor plan. It shows one ascent and one descent. After checking today's openings and storing bags at the entrance, go to the third floor without stopping on the second. Visit Gansu Painted Pottery first, continue to Gansu Buddhist Art on the same floor, then descend to the second-floor Gansu Silk Road Civilization gallery and return to the first-floor exit. Prehistoric vessels, religious images and containers, and long-distance movement then appear in sequence without repeated floor changes. Paleontology and Red Gansu are worthwhile, but add only one when interest, energy, and time before closing all support it. If the lift, stairs, or gallery entrances operate differently that day, follow signs and staff. The order can flex; keep the three central galleries.

caption.zh: 门厅确认后先上三楼，依次看彩陶与佛教艺术，再下到二楼看丝路文明；核心路线走完即可离馆。
caption.ja: 入口で確認して三階へ上がり、彩陶、仏教芸術を見てから二階のシルクロード文明へ下る。核心を終えれば退出してよい。
caption.en: After checking at the entrance, go to the third floor for Painted Pottery and Buddhist Art, descend to the second-floor Silk Road gallery, then leave when the core route is complete.

p.src: Do not begin the Painted Pottery gallery by hunting for its most famous object. Stop at one vessel and look in four passes, as the four guides do here. First, read form alone: how mouth, neck, body, handles, and base work together. Second, follow the black painted lines around the volume without rushing to turn every mark into mythology. Third, read the cultural type and approximate date. Last, find the findspot and locate its county or site within Gansu. If the human-head-mouth vessel is displayed, notice how the sculpted head becomes the opening, then how curved bands respond to the rounded body. If it is absent, use another vessel and keep the method. Four notes in a small notebook will preserve more than a hurried photograph of every case.

caption.zh: 在一件彩陶前依次看器形、图案、类型或年代、出土地；解释放在这些信息之后。
caption.ja: 一つの彩陶で器形、文様、型式または年代、出土地の順に確かめ、解釈はその後に置く。
caption.en: At one painted vessel, read form, pattern, type or date, and findspot in that order; interpretation comes afterwards.

p.src: Two painted vessels are useful precisely because they should not be merged. The human-head-mouth vessel is assigned to the Yangshao Miaodigou type, about 5,500 years ago, and was found at Dadiwan in Qin'an. The salamander-design bottle is assigned to the Yangshao Shilingxia type, about 5,200 years ago, and came from Xiping in Gangu. The first joins a sculpted head, vessel mouth, and black-painted body. The second paints a curved salamander with a long tail across a bottle with two handles. Together they show the complexity of painted-pottery form and design in Gansu; they do not establish one settlement, one period, or one belief. Separate type, date, and place before comparing choices of form. When the label does not explain a motif's symbolism, keep it as a question rather than manufacturing an answer.

p.src: In the Buddhist Art gallery, do not let the phrase “East meets West” do the work of looking. If the fivefold reliquary from Dayun Temple in Jingchuan is displayed, examine how five containers dated to 694 nest: stone casket, gilt-bronze box, silver coffin, gold coffin, and glass relic bottle. Material, scale, and the order from outside to inside are evidence. If the Song *Repaying Parents Sutra* transformation painting from Dunhuang's Library Cave is displayed, look at how a preaching assembly and successive narrative scenes share one silk surface. The two works differ in findspot, date, material, and use. There is no need to hunt for both in order to complete the gallery. Read one carefully and religious practice becomes material: protected through containers or made visible through images. Then return Jingchuan or Dunhuang to the map.

p.src: Wait until the Silk Road gallery to discuss movement; the evidence then becomes specific. If the Han bronze galloping horse is displayed, find it under the museum's official title. Three legs lift clear while one foot rests on a flying bird, fixing speed in bronze through a single support. It came from the Leitai tomb in Wuwei; this guide does not identify the bird as a swallow. Then look, if available, for the Wei-Jin messenger mural brick from Tomb 5 at Jiayuguan. The rider holds a *qizhuan* travel document used at passes and relay stations. The horse turns speed into a funerary bronze. The messenger's document reveals a system of checkpoints and relay stations: travel depended on more than a fast mount. Neither object is a map of the Silk Road, but together they make a route tangible as bodies, mounts, credentials, and places where passage was checked. If only one is present, one is enough.

p.src: The blue diamond marks the museum in Lanzhou; it is not the findspot of any selected object. Numbers 1 and 2 lie to the southeast at Qin'an and Gangu for the painted vessels. Number 3 lies east at Jingchuan for the Dayun Temple reliquary. Number 4 is northwest at Leitai in Wuwei; 5 lies farther west for the messenger brick's Jiayuguan context; 6 sits at Dunhuang for the Library Cave painting. No route joins the numbers because these counties and cities are not one post-museum itinerary. The cases gather objects in Lanzhou while their historical places remain dispersed across the province. After leaving, investigate only a place that lies on your actual onward journey. Leave the others on the map.

caption.zh: 蓝色菱形是兰州的博物馆；六个编号是文物出土地的县市方位，不是要一次走完的路线。
caption.ja: 青い菱形は蘭州の博物館、六つの番号は資料の出土地に対応する県・市の方角であり、一度に巡る経路ではない。
caption.en: The blue diamond is the museum in Lanzhou; the six numbers mark county or city anchors for object findspots, not a route to complete in one trip.

p.src: When rotation, a loan, or temporary removal takes a famous object off display, do not circle the gallery searching for the same name. Choose any object with a useful label and ask four questions. What kind of object or image is it? What date or cultural type does the label assign? Where was it found or collected? What can you verify directly: form, material, working traces, or pattern? Keep “the label states” and “I infer” in separate notebook columns. When photography is permitted, take one overall view without flash and one label image. When it is not, copy the exact title and findspot. This method keeps the route intact without star objects and prevents a shop nickname, a guide's stock phrase, or a personal association from becoming the museum's conclusion.

p.src: After the three central galleries, pause. If energy and a specific interest remain, add either Paleontology or Red Gansu; otherwise return to the first floor. Before leaving, divide the notebook into three columns: what became clear, where the object came from, and what to investigate on the next leg. Leave one question that will change how you see the next place. For example: “At Leitai in Wuwei, how will the tomb context change my view of the bronze horse?” A meal, a hotel rest, or booked transport is more useful than checking off one more gallery before closing.
